title: ESO Guideline 2025: Visual Impairment in Stroke

recommendations.classNote: For; QUADAS-2 medium risk of bias; no GRADE certainty assigned
recommendations.text: Screen adults after stroke with a validated vision tool or specialist eye assessment. Compared with routine stroke screening, vision screening detects more visual impairment; specialist examination further improves detection accuracy.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 1; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: For adults with stroke-related visual problems, evidence is insufficient to recommend early vision screening on activities or quality-of-life outcomes. The source strength is not assessable.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 2; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Screen vision early after stroke. Assessment is feasible and acceptable around days 3–4, and most patients can be assessed within one week. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 2; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Use specialist eye-team assessment or, at minimum, a validated vision-screening tool. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 2; consensus 2

recommendations.classNote: QUADAS-2 medium risk of bias; no GRADE certainty assigned
recommendations.text: For stroke-related visual-field loss, evidence is insufficient to recommend vision screening or specialist eye assessment over routine stroke screening for detection and daily-life outcomes. Recommendation strength is not assessable.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 3; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Screen early for visual-field loss, using specialist eye assessment or at least a validated tool. Assessment around days 3–4 is feasible; most patients can be assessed within one week. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 3; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Dedicated vision screening improves visual-field-loss detection compared with routine stroke screening, and specialist assessment further improves accuracy. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 3; consensus 2

recommendations.classNote: QUADAS-2 medium risk of bias; no GRADE certainty assigned
recommendations.text: For stroke-related central visual impairment, evidence is insufficient to recommend vision screening or specialist eye assessment over routine stroke screening for detection and daily-life outcomes. Strength is not assessable.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 4; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Screen early for central vision or visual-acuity loss through specialist eye assessment or a validated screening tool. Days 3–4 are feasible, and most patients can be assessed within one week. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 4; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Dedicated screening detects central visual impairment better than routine stroke screening; specialist visual assessment further improves accuracy. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 4; consensus 2

recommendations.classNote: QUADAS-2 medium risk of bias; no GRADE certainty assigned
recommendations.text: For post-stroke eye-movement disorders, evidence is insufficient to recommend vision screening or specialist eye assessment over routine stroke screening for detection and daily-life outcomes. Strength is not assessable.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 5; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Screen for eye-movement disorders early using specialist assessment or a validated tool. Assessment around days 3–4 is feasible, with most patients assessed within one week. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 5; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Vision screening detects eye-movement disorders better than routine stroke screening, while specialist visual assessment improves accuracy further. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 5; consensus 2

recommendations.classNote: QUADAS-2 medium risk of bias; no GRADE certainty assigned
recommendations.text: For stroke-related visual perceptual disorders, evidence is insufficient to recommend screening or specialist eye assessment over routine stroke screening for detection and daily-life outcomes. Strength is not assessable.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 6; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Screen early for visual perceptual problems through specialist assessment or a validated vision tool. Days 3–4 are feasible and most patients can be assessed within one week. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 6; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Dedicated screening improves detection of visual perceptual disorders compared with routine stroke screening; specialist assessment improves accuracy further. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 6; consensus 2

recommendations.classNote: For; QUADAS-2 high risk of bias; no GRADE certainty assigned
recommendations.text: Screen adults after stroke for visual neglect. Dedicated vision screening detects more neglect than routine stroke screening; specialist visual assessment and a battery of tests further improve diagnostic accuracy.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 7; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Use compensatory visual-scanning or visual-search training to support adaptation to post-stroke visual-field loss. Begin as soon as feasible and acceptable to the patient.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 8; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: The 2025 guideline suggests thrombolysis within 4.5 hours of onset for central retinal artery occlusion to aid visual recovery; this is a weak recommendation based on very-low-certainty evidence.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 9; recommendation 1
recommendations.currentEvidenceNote: Newer evidence reviewed 2026-09-06: THEIA (2025) did not demonstrate a significant visual benefit from alteplase and was underpowered. TenCRAOS (2026) found no significant visual-recovery benefit from tenecteplase versus aspirin, with serious safety concerns including fatal intracranial haemorrhage. The source guideline's 2025 weak suggestion is historical and should not be read as a current endorsement of routine CRAO thrombolysis.

recommendations.text: For central visual impairment after stroke, evidence is insufficient to recommend compensatory, substitutive or restorative interventions. Recommendation strength is not assessable.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 10; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Offer measures to improve visual acuity as soon as possible after stroke onset. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 10; consensus 1

recommendations.text: Ensure stroke survivors use their prescribed spectacles; promptly replace or update lost, broken or outdated glasses. Direct patients to suitable information, resources and visual aids. Consensus 10/10.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 10; consensus 2

recommendations.text: Individualise treatment to the specific eye-movement disorder and refer to specialist eye services. While awaiting care, partial or total eye occlusion may relieve troublesome diplopia; use total occlusion cautiously because monocular vision loses visual input from the covered eye.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 11; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Individualise treatment to the neglect syndrome, with close collaboration among the stroke team, particularly occupational therapy, neuropsychology and eye services including orthoptics and ophthalmology.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 12; recommendation 1

recommendations.text: Individualise treatment to the specific perceptual problem and direct patients to relevant vision information and resources. Coordinate stroke care, particularly occupational therapy, with neuropsychology, orthoptics and ophthalmology.
recommendations.sourceReference: Table 14, table27-23969873251314693; PICO 1–13 formal and numbered consensus statements; PICO 13; recommendation 1
